front: What are the main forces that can act on a performer?
back: Weight; Reaction force; Friction; Air resistance.

front: What is weight?
back: The force acting on a body due to gravity; it acts vertically downwards through the centre of mass.

front: What is the formula for weight?
back: Weight = Mass × Gravitational acceleration (W = mg).

front: What is reaction force?
back: A force exerted by a surface or body in response to a force applied to it.

front: What is ground reaction force?
back: The force exerted by the ground on a performer in response to the force the performer applies to the ground.

front: How can ground reaction force help a performer?
back: The performer applies force against the ground and the ground exerts an equal and opposite reaction force; e.g. a sprinter pushes backwards and downwards against the ground and the ground reaction force helps propel them forwards and upwards.

front: What is friction?
back: A force that opposes the motion or attempted motion between two surfaces in contact.

front: How can friction benefit a performer?
back: It provides grip between the performer and the surface; e.g. a sprinter's spikes increase friction with the track and reduce slipping.

front: How can friction negatively affect a performer?
back: It can oppose movement, reducing speed and increasing the energy required to maintain motion.

front: What is air resistance?
back: A drag force that opposes the motion of a body as it moves through the air.

front: What factors affect air resistance?
back: Velocity of the performer; Frontal cross-sectional area; Shape and surface characteristics.

front: How does velocity affect air resistance?
back: As the velocity of a performer increases, air resistance increases.

front: How does frontal cross-sectional area affect air resistance?
back: A larger frontal cross-sectional area increases air resistance, while a smaller frontal cross-sectional area reduces it.

front: How can a performer reduce air resistance?
back: Adopt a streamlined body position; Reduce frontal cross-sectional area; Use aerodynamic clothing or equipment.

front: Why might reducing air resistance improve performance?
back: Less force opposes the performer's motion, allowing them to maintain a greater velocity or use less energy.

front: What is a vector?
back: A quantity that has both magnitude and direction.

front: How are vectors represented?
back: By arrows that show the magnitude and direction of a quantity.

front: What does magnitude mean?
back: The size of a force or quantity.

front: How is magnitude shown on a vector diagram?
back: By the length of the arrow; a longer arrow represents a greater magnitude.

front: What does direction mean?
back: The direction in which a force acts or a body moves.

front: What shows direction on a vector?
back: The arrowhead shows the direction in which the vector acts.

front: What is the line of application?
back: The imaginary straight line along which a force acts.

front: What is the point of application?
back: The point at which a force is applied to a body.

front: What is velocity?
back: The rate of change of displacement.

front: What is the formula for velocity?
back: Velocity = Displacement ÷ Time.

front: What is the key difference between speed and velocity?
back: Velocity is a vector quantity and includes direction, whereas speed is a scalar quantity and has magnitude only.

front: What is displacement and what is its unit?
back: The straight-line distance from the starting position to the finishing position in a specified direction; measured in metres (m).

front: What is velocity? Give its formula and unit.
back: The rate of change of displacement; Velocity = Displacement ÷ Time; measured in metres per second (m/s).

front: What is momentum? Give its formula and unit.
back: The quantity of motion possessed by a moving body; Momentum = Mass × Velocity (p = mv); measured in kg·m/s.

front: What is acceleration? Give its formula and unit.
back: The rate of change of velocity; Acceleration = Change in velocity ÷ Time; measured in metres per second squared (m/s²).

front: What is mass?
back: The quantity of matter in a body.

front: What unit is mass measured in?
back: Kilograms (kg).

front: What is speed?
back: The distance travelled per unit of time.

front: What is the formula for speed?
back: Speed = Distance ÷ Time.

front: What does a horizontal line on a distance-time graph show?
back: The object is stationary, so no distance is being covered.

front: What does a straight diagonal line on a distance-time graph show?
back: The object is moving at a constant speed.

front: What does a curve becoming steeper on a distance-time graph show?
back: The object's speed is increasing, showing acceleration.

front: What does a curve becoming less steep on a distance-time graph show?
back: The object's speed is decreasing, showing deceleration.

front: What does the gradient of a distance-time graph represent?
back: Speed.

front: What does a zero gradient on a distance-time graph mean?
back: The object is stationary.

front: What does a constant gradient on a distance-time graph mean?
back: The object is moving at a constant speed.

front: What does an increasing gradient on a distance-time graph mean?
back: The object's speed is increasing.

front: What does a decreasing gradient on a distance-time graph mean?
back: The object's speed is decreasing.

front: What is impulse?
back: The change in momentum produced when a force acts over a period of time.

front: What is the equation for impulse?
back: Impulse = Force × Time.

front: What does impulse measure?
back: The effect of a force acting on an object over a period of time, resulting in a change in momentum.

front: What are the units of impulse?
back: Newton seconds (Ns).

front: How does impulse link to Newton's First Law?
back: A change in an object's state of motion occurs when an external resultant force acts on it.

front: How does impulse link to Newton's Second Law?
back: Impulse is equal to the change in momentum, so a greater impulse produces a greater change in momentum.

front: What happens to the change in momentum when impulse increases?
back: The change in momentum increases.

front: What effect can an increased impulse have on velocity?
back: It can produce a greater change in velocity.

front: How can impulse be increased to produce a greater change in momentum?
back: Increase the force applied.

front: How else can impulse be increased to produce a greater change in momentum?
back: Increase the time over which the force is applied.

front: How can impulse principles be used to reduce the force experienced when decreasing momentum?
back: Increase the time over which the change in momentum occurs, reducing the average force experienced.

front: Why does increasing the time of impact reduce the average force experienced?
back: The same change in momentum occurs over a longer period of time, so a smaller average force is required.

front: What does the area under a force-time graph represent?
back: Impulse.

front: What does a large positive impulse represent on a force-time graph?
back: A large positive change in momentum.

front: When does positive impulse occur during sprinting?
back: During propulsion, when the athlete applies force backwards against the ground and is propelled forwards.

front: What does a negative impulse represent on a force-time graph?
back: A decrease in forward momentum.

front: When does negative impulse occur during sprinting?
back: During the braking phase immediately after the foot contacts the ground, when the ground reaction force acts to reduce forward momentum.

front: What does a small impulse indicate?
back: A small change in momentum.

front: What is a free-body diagram?
back: A diagram showing all the external forces acting on an object or performer.

front: Where is weight drawn from on a free-body diagram?
back: From the object's or performer's centre of mass.

front: In which direction does weight act?
back: Vertically downwards towards the centre of the Earth.

front: Where does a reaction force act from?
back: The point of contact between two bodies or surfaces.

front: What is friction?
back: A force that opposes the motion or attempted motion between two surfaces in contact.

front: Where does friction act from?
back: The point of contact between the two surfaces.

front: In which direction does friction act?
back: Opposite to the direction of motion or attempted motion between the surfaces.

front: How is friction drawn relative to the direction of motion?
back: In the opposite direction to the motion or attempted motion.

front: What is air resistance?
back: A drag force that opposes the movement of an object or performer through the air.

front: Where is air resistance drawn from on a free-body diagram?
back: From the centre of mass.

front: In which direction does air resistance act?
back: Opposite to the direction of motion through the air.

front: What does AR stand for on a free-body diagram?
back: Air resistance.

front: Why is the length of an arrow important on a free-body diagram?
back: It represents the magnitude of the force; a longer arrow represents a greater force.

front: What is net force?
back: The resultant force acting on an object after all the individual forces have been combined.

front: What does a net force of zero mean?
back: The forces are balanced, so there is no acceleration and the object remains at rest or continues moving at constant velocity.

front: What happens when forces are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction?
back: The forces are balanced and the resultant force is zero.

front: What is the result of balanced forces?
back: There is zero net force, so there is no acceleration and the object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity.

front: What happens if the upward reaction force is greater than the downward weight force?
back: There is a resultant upward force, causing the performer to accelerate upwards.
